passage: Irfan, listen. I'm Akash. When I was twenty, my roommate Bhaskar came back from his first mountain trek, and I asked, "Did you like it?" "Yes," he said, and that was that. The next time he went, I tried something else. I said, "How did that feel, standing up there?" He put his bag down and sat on my bed. "Quiet," he said. "Strange. I wanted to shout, but I couldn't, and my knees hurt." Then he told me about the fog, and the old man who shared his tea, and the moment he nearly turned back. We talked till the light in the corridor was switched off. I never asked a yes-or-no question about his trips again.

qa.q: What did Akash ask Bhaskar the first time?
qa.a: "Did you like it?"

qa.q: What did Bhaskar seem to be feeling as he set the bag down and talked about standing up there?
qa.a: Reflective and moved. Bhaskar described the quiet and the wish to shout, and shared the moment of nearly turning back.

qa.q: What choice by Akash led to the fuller story?
qa.a: Akash changed from a yes-or-no question to "How did that feel, standing up there?", which invited Bhaskar to tell it.

qa.q: How might Bhaskar have felt about the two questions?
qa.a: The first probably felt like a box to tick; the second felt like real interest, which is why Bhaskar sat down and talked for a long time.

grounding: A young adult asks a roommate how did that feel instead of a yes-or-no question, and gets a fuller answer.

passage: On the crowded platform, with the train due in five minutes and a loudspeaker crackling over everything, Amandeep spotted Siddharth coming out of the audition hall. Earlier, Amandeep had already asked, "Was it fun?" and got a shrug and a "Yes." Now, over the noise, Amandeep asked, "How did that feel, when you started to sing?" Siddharth stopped walking. "My voice shook at first," said Siddharth. "Then I heard the teacher tapping the beat, and I felt safe. It was the first time I enjoyed it." The train rolled in. "Tell me more on the way," said Amandeep, and they boarded together.

qa.q: How much time was left before the train came?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when starting to sing, and what changed?
qa.a: Nervous, since the voice shook at first, then safe and happy once hearing the teacher tap the beat.

qa.q: What choice by Amandeep got a fuller answer, even in a noisy place?
qa.a: Amandeep asked "How did that feel, when you started to sing?" instead of repeating a yes-or-no question.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt on getting only a shrug and a "Yes" the first time?
qa.a: Probably unsatisfied and still curious, which is why Amandeep asked a more open question over the noise.

grounding: A young adult asks how did that feel rather than a yes-or-no question and gets a fuller answer, even under time pressure.

passage: At the chai stall outside the Gurugram metro, Seema caught up with her friend Ujjwal after his first week at the new internship. "So, did you like it?" she asked. "Yeah. It was fine." Seema waited. Nothing else came. She tried again. "Okay, but what was it like walking in on the first day?" Ujjwal laughed and put down his cup. "Honestly? Terrifying. Everyone was in suits and I was in a checked shirt. My manager called me by the wrong name for two days. And then on Thursday, she asked for my idea in a meeting, and they actually used it." He talked for twenty minutes: the canteen, the lift that stopped on every floor, the colleague who lent him a charger. Walking home, Seema thought about it. "Did you like it?" had got one word. "What was it like?" had got a story.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal wearing on his first day?
qa.a: A checked shirt.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as he described his first week?
qa.a: He felt a mix of fear and pride, calling the first day terrifying but lighting up when his idea was used.

qa.q: Why did Seema's second question work better?
qa.a: It was open and curious, asking what the day was like instead of a yes-or-no question, so Ujjwal could tell a full story.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had stopped after 'Did you like it?'
qa.a: She would have heard only 'fine' and missed the fear, the wrong name and the idea that got used.

grounding: Shows a young adult switching from a closed question to an open one and getting a much fuller answer from a friend.

passage:
"Nikita! You're back from the trek! Did you have fun?"
"Yeah, it was good."
Damini waited. "Just good?"
"Mm."
Damini tried again. "What was the hardest part?"
Nikita paused. "The last climb. It was so steep, I nearly turned back. I cried a bit, actually."
"Really? What made you keep going?"
"There was this old man in our group, like sixty-five, who just kept saying, 'Chhota kadam, chhota kadam.' Small steps. So I did."
"And what was it like at the top?"
Nikita's face lit up. "Quiet. Like, totally quiet. I sat there and felt like my brain finally switched off."
Damini grinned. "That's way more than 'good.'"
"You asked better questions," Nikita laughed.

qa.q: What did the old man in Nikita's group keep saying?
qa.a: 'Chhota kadam, chhota kadam.' Small steps.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling at the top of the climb?
qa.a: Nikita felt calm and peaceful, as if the brain had finally switched off.

qa.q: What made Damini's later questions work better than 'Did you have fun?'
qa.a: They were open and specific, like 'What was the hardest part?', inviting Nikita to tell a story instead of just agreeing.

qa.q: What would change if Damini had accepted 'it was good'?
qa.a: Damini would never have heard about the steep climb, the old man's 'small steps' or the quiet at the top.

grounding: Shows a young adult using open, curious questions to get a friend's full story instead of one-word answers.

passage:
After Ritu's dance audition, I used to ask, "Did it go well?" She'd say, "Yeah, I think so," and that was it. I thought she just didn't want to talk.
Then my cousin, who's a counsellor, told me I was asking questions that only needed a yes. So after Ritu's next audition, I tried something different. "What was it like, being up there?"
She sat down on my bed. "My legs were shaking. But when the music started, I forgot everyone. Except one judge who kept yawning. That made me so angry I danced harder." She laughed. "I think it was my best ever."
She talked for almost an hour. I'd never heard any of that before.
I'm Rehana. I still catch myself asking yes-or-no questions. But now I notice.

qa.q: What did one judge keep doing during Ritu's audition?
qa.a: The judge kept yawning.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel during the audition?
qa.a: Her legs were shaking with nerves at first, then she felt angry at the yawning judge and danced harder, feeling it was her best ever.

qa.q: What small change did Rehana make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rehana asked 'What was it like?' instead of 'Did it go well?', which invited Ritu to tell a real story.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana kept asking yes-or-no questions?
qa.a: Ritu would probably keep answering 'yeah, I think so', and Rehana would miss the real stories.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning that open, curious questions invite a friend's full story while closed ones invite a short yes.

passage: Coordinator's note, peer-listening circle, hostel common room, Thursday. Pairs practised talking about something recent. Sangeeta's partner, Ira, had just returned from her first solo trip to Shillong. Sangeeta began with "Did you like it?" Ira said, "Yeah, it was nice," and stopped. Sangeeta glanced at the prompt card, paused, and tried again: "What did it feel like, being there on your own?" Ira sat back. She described missing the bus on the first day, panicking at the stand, then eating momos with a stranger's family who helped her find the right route. She laughed while telling it and said she had not told anyone that part. The whole answer took nearly four minutes, against four seconds for the first. Afterwards Sangeeta told the group that the first question already had its answer tucked inside it. Next session I will ask every pair to swap one yes-or-no question for a "how" question and notice what changes.

qa.q: Where had Ira just returned from?
qa.a: Ira had just returned from her first solo trip to Shillong.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta pause and try a second question?
qa.a: Sangeeta seemed a little uneasy that "it was nice" had ended the talk so fast, and curious to hear more, so she tried a question that could not be answered with a yes.

qa.q: What small step does the coordinator plan for the next session?
qa.a: Every pair will swap one yes-or-no question for a "how" question and notice what changes, which is a simple, kind way to practise 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Ira when the second question came?
qa.a: Ira got room to tell the real story, the panic at the bus stand and the kind strangers, instead of just agreeing that the trip was nice.

grounding: Shows a young adult swapping a closed "did you like it" question for an open question about how the trip felt and getting a much fuller story.
